title: DFS / flood fill
summary: Depth-first search follows one path as far as it goes before backing up. Flood fill uses it to mark a whole connected region, so counting regions is counting how many fills you start.
idea: Scan every cell. Each unvisited land cell starts a new region: count it, then DFS to mark every cell joined to it, so the scan never counts it again.

signals.see: Count islands, rooms, blobs, provinces or connected groups.
signals.think: Loop over every cell or node. Each one not yet visited starts a DFS that marks its whole group; the number of DFS starts is the answer.

signals.see: Paint, fill or capture a connected area, like a paint bucket tool.
signals.think: DFS from the clicked cell and recolour every neighbour with the old colour. Mark cells as you go so none is painted twice.

signals.see: The answer depends on the size, shape or border of each region.
signals.think: Have the DFS return or count the cells it marks. Track anything else you need, such as touching the edge, during the same fill.

phrasings: A satellite photo is a grid of land and water. How many separate islands are there?
Clicking a pixel with the fill tool recolours every touching pixel of the same colour. Return the new image.
Regions of O fully surrounded by X are captured. Which cells flip?

picture.title: Counting land cells versus sinking whole islands
picture.alt: On the left, counting each land cell gives the number of land cells, not islands, because one island has many cells. On the right, each new land cell starts a depth-first fill that marks its whole island, so the scan counts each island exactly once.
picture.caption: Mark the whole region the moment you find it, and later cells of it are skipped.

after.label: Pattern: count, then sink with DFS

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 5 rows separated by /, each with up to 5 values: 1 is land and 0 is water. Every row needs the same number of values.

oneLiner: for each cell: if unvisited land, count += 1 and DFS-mark every connected land cell

exercise.prompt: A map is a grid where 1 is land and 0 is water. Land cells join when they share a side. Return the number of cells in the largest island, or 0 if there is no land. The starter only explores down and right, so it splits islands that bend up or left.
hints: Each unvisited land cell starts a new island. Fill it with DFS and count the cells you mark.
Check all four neighbours. An island can snake up and to the left of where you first found it.
A large island can be thousands of cells deep. In Python, use an explicit stack instead of recursion.

complexity.why: Every cell is scanned once and marked at most once, and each mark checks four neighbours. In the worst case, one snake-shaped island puts every cell on the stack or call stack.

mistakes: Forgetting to mark a cell before exploring from it, so two neighbours keep calling each other forever.
Checking only some directions, which splits one island into several.
Recursing on a 1,000 × 1,000 grid in Python and hitting the recursion limit. Use an explicit stack.
Changing the input grid when the caller still needs it. Copy it, or keep a separate seen grid.

quiz.question: In the island count, why does count go up only when the scan finds unvisited land?
choices: Because each fill marks the whole island, so its other cells are already visited
quiz.explain: The first cell of each island triggers a fill that marks all of it, so the scan skips the rest.

quiz.question: What stops the fill from looping forever between two land cells?
choices: Marking each cell before or as it is explored
quiz.explain: A marked cell fails the land check, so neighbours do not call each other again.

quiz.question: A grid is 2,000 × 2,000 and fully land. What can go wrong with a recursive fill?
choices: The call stack can reach 4 million frames and overflow
BFS would give a different count
quiz.explain: Recursion depth can equal the island size. An explicit stack or BFS avoids the limit.

interviewTip: Mention the recursion depth before the interviewer does. Offer the recursive version for clarity and say you would switch to an explicit stack for large grids.
